title: About
text:
The first mini project was about simulation and used many techniques that we saw later on in the course. It was the first time we looped through a function which we did many times later with both bootstrapping and empirical power tests. We also used many density functions that we worked with a lot throughout the semester such as the exponential and beta distribution. My biggest takeaway form mini project 1 was probably how useful simulation can be in statistics and I thoguth it was cool that the theoretcial results were closely matched with the simulated results,
The second mini project was about showing our understanding of different statistical terms and to use them in context of a meaningful story. This is something that has been important throughout the course as we have been prompted to interpret results in context of a problem and explain certain statistical terms or techniques in plain English throughout the course. This project really made me think about the meaning of the terms we had been using so far in the semester and it challenged my understanding of the concepts in a good wat.
This project was somewhat similar to mini project 5 where we answered questions based of an article arguing that relying on arbitrary thresholds for p-value is not statistically sounds. Both these projects were geared towards a higher level understanding of concepts than actual calculations. I had many takeaways from this article and the put a lot of thoguht into my answers. Something that will stick with me is when the authors said that there is no signification difference between a significant and insignificant test.
Mini project 3 was about confidence interval assumptions and brought back some simulation techniques such as looping through a fucntion from mini project 1. This project showcased the importance of assumptions and the consequences if assumptions are broken, something that we have talked about hroguhout the course and something I remember talking about in stat 113. This project was important to show how results can differ when assumptions are broken and it tied into mini project 4 about Bayesian analysis well. In mini project 4 we worked with different prior distributions to reach a posterior distribution and it was important to know what assumptions each prior distribution was believing to be true. Apart from the assumption and interpreting in context part of mini project 4, it kind of stood out among the projects as it was the only project where we did not with frequentist statistics.
For this option, you will create a Quarto Blog/Website containing your 5 mini-projects, and write a reflection that ties the mini-projects together and gives biggest take-aways from each project.
Your reflection should either go in the about.qmd file that appears at the root directory of the R Project, the index.qmd file that also appears at the root directory of the R Project, or in a separate blog post. The rendered .html file from about.qmd essentially serves as the home page for the blog. The reflection should be about 5 paragraphs or so and should address:

how each mini-project ties in to other content in the course.
how each mini-project ties in with some other mini-projects (note that some mini-projects are more connected than others: you do not need to “connect” every single mini-project with every other mini-project).
your biggest take-aways from these mini-projects (these should not be copy-pasted from the “take-away” section of any of your original mini-projects: the expectation is that, now that we have gone through the entire course, your take-aways may be more sophisticated now).

Some extra notes:

mini-project 1 is the only mini-project that had substantial handwritten work. You do not need to include the handwritten derivations in the blog.
if, for other mini-projects, you have things that you submitted that you wrote by hand, you can embed these as images in quarto using knitr::include_graphics("path_to_image.jpg").
as you are creating your five posts for the five mini-projects, note that the .qmd file must be named index.qmd within each folder and that the folder itself cannot have any spaces or special characters in its name.

title: Mini Project 3: Confidence Interval Assumptions
text:
Large N, p = 0.9

n <- 250   # sample size
p <- 0.9  # population proportion
  
generate_samp_prop <- function(n, p) {
  x <- rbinom(1, n, p) # randomly generate number of successes for the sample
  
  ## number of successes divided by sample size
  phat <- x / n
  
  # 90% CI
  lb <- phat - 1.645 * sqrt(phat * (1- phat) / n)
  ub <- phat + 1.645 * sqrt(phat * (1- phat) / n)
  
  # return df with sample proportion, lower and upper bounds of CI for that sample
  prop_df <- tibble(phat, lb, ub)
  return(prop_df)
}

generate_samp_prop(n = 250, p = 0.9)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
   phat    lb    ub

prop_ci_df <- map(1:nsim, 
    \(i) generate_samp_prop(n = 250, p = 0.9)) |> bind_rows()

title: Mini Project 3: Confidence Interval Assumptions
text:
Findings
This project showed me how the theoretical assumptions of confidence intervals work and how they connect to real-life scenarios. It is clear that with a very big n, such as n = 250, the asymptotic confidence interval holds. Intuitively I was surprised that the coverage rate was higher for n = 25 than for n = 250 when p = 0.9. However, I realized that this was because the average width of the interval got wider as n decreased, since the margin of error formula includes division by n. A wider interval has a higher chance of capturing p, leading to a higher coverage rate.
I also thought it was interesting that the average width of the interval was smaller for p = 0.9 than for p = 0.47. This is because the standard error is bigger when p = 0.47 since 0.47(1-0.47) > 0.9(1-0.9). However, this does not always translate to a higher coverage rate for p = 0.47 which we can see for n = 25.
Another interesting takeaway for me was that when the large sample assumtpion is broken but the data is approximately normal, it seems like the asymptotic confidence interval is still relatively correct. For example, the large sample assumption is broken for n = 10 and p = 0.47 but the coverage rate is still close to 0.9. Compared to when n = 10 and p = 0.9, since binom with p = 0.9 is skeewed, the small n is not enough to make up for this skewness and the coverage rate is only 0.63. Overall, this project helped me understand not just why the assumptions matter, but also how breaking them affects the accuracy of confidence intervals in different ways.

## create population graphs

norm_df <- tibble(x = seq(3, 17, length.out = 1000),
                  dens = dnorm(x, mean = 10, sd = 2),
                  pop = "normal(10, 4)")
unif_df <- tibble(x = seq(7, 13, length.out = 1000),
                  dens = dunif(x, 7, 13),
                  pop = "uniform(7, 13)")
exp_df <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 1000),
                 dens = dexp(x, 0.5),
                 pop = "exp(0.5)")
beta_df <- tibble(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000),
                  dens = dbeta(x, 8, 2),
                  pop = "beta(8, 2)")

pop_plot <- bind_rows(norm_df, unif_df, exp_df, beta_df) |>
  mutate(pop = fct_relevel(pop, c("normal(10, 4)", "uniform(7, 13)",
                                  "exp(0.5)", "beta(8, 2)")))

ggplot(data = pop_plot, aes(x = x, y = dens)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~ pop, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Population Distributions for Each Simulation Setting")

For the normal distribution with mu = 10 and sigma = 2, the distribution of the sample minimum and maximum when n = 5 have roughly the same Standard Error which makes sense becuase they both come from a normally distributed population.
For the Uniform distribution with theta one = 7 and theta 2 = 13, the distribution of the sample minimum and maximum when n = 5 have roughly the same Standard Error also. This is also apparent when you look at the distributions respective graphs, they have the same skewed shape but are basically mirrored versions of each other.
For the exponential distribution with lambda = 0.5, the distributions of the sample minimum and maximum when n = 5 have different Standard Errors. The Standard Error for the Sample Minimum distribution is much smaller than the Standard Error for the Sample Maximum distribution. This can be seen visually when comparing the histograms of the sample minimum and maximum distributions as the sample maximum looks like a more stretched out version of the sample minimum distribution.
I also think this is intuitive when looking at the graph of the population distribution. There’s more density towards the lower values, so more of the minimums will be sampled close to and it will create a right-skewed distribution with a lot of density close to 0. The density of the maximum will be more spread out considering the shape of the population graph, which we also can see in the histogram od the sample maximum distribution. I expect this to hold for a similar population to the one we tested with.
For the beta distribution with alpha = 8 and beta = 2, the distributions of the sample minimum and maximum when n = 5 have different Standard Errors. This time it’s the other way around and the Standard Error for the Sample Minimum is bigger than the Standard Error for the Sample Maximum Distribution.
When comparing the population graphs between the Beta and Exponential population I belive you can see why this is the result. The Beta graph has low density close to 0 and then it accelrates around 0.5 up to almost 1. This for me means that the sample minimum might be spread out while the sample maximum might be more concentrated which we also can see in their repsective graphs. I also expect this to hold for a similar population to the one we tested with.

title: Mini Project 2: A Meaningful Story
text:
Growing up on a horse farm in Sweden I have always been used to being around animals. I helped my mom walk the horses, fill up water, measure up food, keep equipment clean, and much more. But I was never a big fan of horses myself, I thought they took too much time to take care of and that they didn’t give you much back. This could also be because my dad is terrified of horses and tried his best to get me and my brother interested in racket sports, soccer, and motor vehicles like our tractor, atv, and dirt bikes. His tactic worked and we never became horse riders. However, we were still animal lovers and wanted our own animals. We had many discussions on what we should get. Sheep? No, they smell bad and the likelihood of them running away and causing problems is too high. Cows? Too much work. Pigs? Not that cute. Although I did want a mini pig for a while, I failed to convince my parents. We ended up getting chickens. We got mini-cochins, small chicken with feathers on their feet.
Chicken don’t require too much work, they need clean water, eat all your leftovers, and they give you eggs back as a reward. It was the perfect animal for my brother and I to take care of. We ended up getting 12 chickens and one rooster. They became very tame as my brother and I would pet them a lot and once they grew up, they started producing a lot of eggs.
We soon understood that we had to eat a lot of eggs because they were some very well producing chickens. We had to try and estimate the random variable of how many eggs 12 chicken produce in a day. This required some training and there were many parameters in play such as the season of the year, what food we gave them, and the cycle they are in. This was harder than we first thought. After observing them for a year, taking random samples and writing them down, we noticed that the number of eggs collected each day seemed to vary randomly between 0 and approximately 0.9n, with no particular number occurring more frequently than another. Since there was no clear central tendency and each value within that range appeared equally likely over time, we assumed the number of eggs per day followed a uniform distribution with theta1=0 and an estimator for theta2​. Our estimator for theta2 was 0.9n because we had never measured one egg per chicken for one day. This produced an estimate of a uniform distribution with an expected value of 5.4 eggs per day.
Unfortunately, some days we got zero eggs, and they could even go weeks with zero eggs. But sometimes we would get over 70 eggs a week. Needless to say, the variance was very high, and it was hard to figure out why. We began to wonder—was our estimator biased? Were we systematically over or underestimating production because we ignored extreme fluctuations? Despite the high variance, our estimator was at least consistent as over long periods, it stabilized around the average number of eggs we collected.
Like all good stories this one also ends in tragedy. Our chickens were roaming free on the farm and in our garden every day. They went into their hut before dusk, and we closed their hatch so no predators could get in. One dark October night, a small, nasty ferret had sneaked through the chicken wire. The morning after we had no chicken left. It was a total devastation for all of us. We had accounted for foxes in our risk assessment but had failed to consider the likelihood of a ferret attack. Our estimation had been incomplete, and we had underestimated the probability of total loss. After that both my brother and I were done raising chicken and we didn’t get new ones again.
However, only a year ago my dad picked it up again and got 6 new chickens that again roam the farm, and the garden, and in a year hopefully will produce eggs. Maybe he will be able to derive a better estimator than we were. After all, we were only 12 and 8 years old trying to derive a maximum likelihood function, maybe not with weird symbols and logs, but with the eggs we collected every day.

title: Mini Project 5: Advantages and Drawbacks of Using p-values
text:
Towards the end of Section 1, the authors say “As ‘statistical significance’ is used less, statistical thinking will be used more.” Elaborate on what you think the authors mean. Give some examples of what you think embodies “statistical thinking.” I think the authors mean that if we stop relying on statistical significance in the traditional way which is having a p-value lower than a somewhat arbitrary threshold, then we will have to be more thorough in our statistical analysis. Some people today believe that showing a p-value < 0.05 automatically means that they have found an effect when there are many things left to consider. If they instead had to show more evidence of this effect, they would have used more statistical techniques, and I think it could increase the understanding of statistics. Some examples of this kind of statistical thinking could be to show where the test statistic falls on the distribution if the null hypothesis is true, discuss if all assumptions are correct and provide some evidence when possible. For example, plot the data to see if CLT holds if it’s used in the hypothesis test. We would also have to get better at interpreting the p-value as a number instead of a categorical variable. What I mean with this is that instead of saying “strong evidence”, “moderate”, or “no evidence”, we would have to interpret what a 0.02 p-value means. I think this definitely requires more statistical thinking.
Section 2, third paragraph: The authors state “A label of statistical significance adds nothing to what is already conveyed by the value of p; in fact, this dichotomization of p-values makes matters worse.” Elaborate on what you think the authors means. I really agree with the point that the authors make here and it’s something that I have struggled with understanding since I first took stat 113. I think the thing that best describes what they mean in this paragraph is “As Gelman and Stern (2006) famously observed, the difference between “significant” and “not significant” is not itself statistically significant. “. For example, if we use a threshold of p < 0.05 and we get a p-value of 0.049 or 0.052, the meaning of these p-values is incredibly similar, and yet if these were two different studies, one of them might have gone unpublished. I even think that these labels for p-values have hurt the scientific community a lot over time as I have read articles about how researchers have manipulated their data to be able to reach a p < 0.05 instead of reporting the p-value they originally would got. This makes replicating results much harder, and it makes the research less credible. If we instead of using labels with hard thresholds just reported the p-value as a number and used statistical thinking as described above, then I think more good research would be published and there would be less bias in what is reported.
Section 2, end of first column: The authors state “For the integrity of scientific publishing and research dissemination, therefore, whether a p-value passes any arbitrary threshold should not be considered at all when deciding which results to present or highlight.” Do you agree or disagree? How should it be decided which results to present/highlight in scientific publishing?

I agree with this. I believe we would get better research if researchers did not choose what to highlight based on a p-value below an arbitrary threshold. If we instead used p-values as the number it is and interpreted it in context of the research, I think it would allow researchers to present more interesting results even if they are not below for example p < 0.05. However, there is of course a problem in that we don’t want research to be published without considering that deviations from the null hypothesis could simply be due to random chance. If researchers highlight results without interpreting p-values carefully, there is a risk of overstating findings that are actually consistent with the null. A better approach would be to present all results transparently, discuss p-values as continuous evidence rather than binary cutoffs. I believe this can lead to more rigorous research and more rigorous control/review before research is published because if we are not dependent on an arbitrary cutoff, then researchers need to provide more evidence to why the effect they have found should be considered.

Section 3, end of page 2: The authors state “The statistical community has not yet converged on a simple paradigm for the use of statistical inference in scientific research – and in fact it may never do so. A one-size-fits-all approach to statistical inference is an inappropriate expectation.” Do you agree or disagree? Explain.

I think this one is tricky because I agree that different studies and different disciplines might benefit from different approaches to statistical inference. For example, in some fields, making a type 1 error is much more serious than it is in other fields and vice versa. However, if every scientist would use their own technique for statistical inference, this would make it very hard to follow research and to know if a publishing shows an interesting effect or not. I believe that the right way to go is something in between of these two extremes. I think the authors explain it well with their ATOM model and I believe that if everyone followed their guidelines, we would get better research. I think it would be good to have some clearer guidelines for what is expected to show in a study when it comes to statistical inference such as effect sizes, clear interpretations of p-values, discussions of assumptions etc. I think the key word in their sentence is “a simple paradigm”, I don’t think statistical inference will nor should ever be simple. There are so many things to consider and making it “simple” would by definition look away from many of the difficulties and uncertainties related to statistical inference. Instead I think the goal should be to make statistical inference robust and replicable even if it requires more work.

Section 3.2: The authors note that they are envisioning “a sort of ‘statistical thoughtfulness’.” What do you think “statistical thoughtfulness” means? What are some ways to demonstrate “statistical thoughtfulness” in an analysis?

I think statistical thoughtfulness can mean a lot of things. I really like how they authors discuss the importance of being clear on if a study is exploratory or planned and the difference it makes. If a study is planned, then I agree that the hypothesis need to be clearly stated at the beginning which I think is praxis anyway. However, what I really liked was the minimal meaningful effect size prior to analyzing data. As an economics major, I find cost-benefit and opportunity costs very interesting, and I believe that having a minimal meaningful effect size would make it easier to argue for a certain intervention after a study. If a researcher says that their study will need an effect of at least x% to be worth the cost and risk of implementing it in for example a school, before the study is began, then I believe their results would be much more credible. Like the authors state, I believe there is a high risk that a researcher argues that the effect they found in their data is enough for it to be implemented. Stating a minimal effect size prior to the study makes a researcher think about the costs and benefits associated to what they are studying and I believe this could make a significant (scary word to use here) difference in the effect of research in real life applications. I also think statistical thoughtfulness can be demonstrated by understanding your data, discussing your model assumptions and if you believe that are fulfilled, and discuss your model specification. This is necessary for any statistical results to be taken seriously. In Econometrics we experimented with different model specifications to better understand the importance of a correctly specified model and the differences really surprised me. The authors also mention the importance of reading and mentioning prior research in the area. I agree that it is important to learn from existing research, to see what we know, and what evidence there is to support those claims. However, when reviewing existing research, I think it’s important to realize that things might have changed since it was published and we need to be critical and thoroughly go through the existing studies and ask ourselves questions such as “do their assumptions still hold?”, and “were their model correctly specified?” etc. I’m surprised that the authors did not mention much about this since they are so critical of a lot of research that is published throughout the paper.

Section 3.2.4: A few of the authors of papers in this special issue argue that some of the terminology used in statistics, such as “significance” and “confidence” can be misleading, and they propose the use of “compatibility” instead. What you do you think they believe the problem is? Do you agree or disagree (that there is a problem and that changing the name will help)? I understand what they mean, especially with significance as it stems from an arbitrarily chosen threshold. I can also find confidence somewhat misleading because it kind of implies there is very little uncertainty when there still can be uncertainty. Also, a lot of people think that a 95% confidence interval means that there is a 95% probability that the true value which is not true. I think they believe that the problem is that using these words and approaches simplifies the approach to statistical inference to a point where thoughtfulness is no longer needed. However, I’m not sure that changing the name of confidence to combability will solve the bigger picture problem. I do agree that combability describes it well, but I believe that even if the name is changed, scientists might still use it in the same way as before. However, interpreting p-values as their number instead of saying significant or not I think would make a bigger change. I also like their idea of testing more than one hypothesis, such as testing it against the predetermined minimal effect size. I think that better statistical education and higher requirements of statistical thoughtfulness during peer review is probably the best approach to moving beyond a world of p < 0.05 and changing names of concepts will not get us there.
Find a quote or point that really strikes you (i.e., made you think). What is the quote (and tell me where to find it), and why does it stand out to you? There were many quotes that stood out to me but the general idea that stood out to me the most was to always declare a minimum effect size before collecting and analyzing data and to test more than one null hypothesis. One example where this is mentioned is 3.2.2 paragraph 3 “Despite these limitations, if you present p-values, do so for more than one hypothesized value of your variable of interest (Fraser 2019; Greenland 2019), such as 0 and at least one plausible, relevant alternative, such as the minimum practically important effect size (which should be determined before analyzing the data).” This makes a lot of sense to me. It has researchers analyze the costs and benefits before conducting their study, it makes the literature review more important since prior research is likely a good place to start for a minimum practically important effect size. I also think it makes sense to look at more than a non-zero effect since a p-value says nothing about how big an effect is, and for research that can be implemented in the real world, effect size matters a lot. I think it can be an important step for planned studies to not slip into the exploratory side since a researcher has not only have to come up with the null hypothesis but also a minimum practically important effect. If this is not done before the study, then I think there is a risk that some researchers would argue for a minimum practically important effect that fits their data instead of doing an unbiased cost and benefit analysis. I think this idea stood out to me because in class we always talk about testing one null and one alternative hypothesis, but this is arguing that we can do more. It also combines the cost/benefit and opportunity cost mindset that is often used in economics with statistics.

title: Mini Project 4: Bayesian Analysis
text:
Project Report
In this project we try to model the probability that Nadal wins a point on his serve when playing on a clay surface. I will answer this question by trying a couple different prior distributions that have different assumptions, combine them with the given data, and compare the three different posterior distributions to see which one I think best models the data.
typed work justifying the decisions you made to create the two informative priors. What did you assume when you made those priors?
For the first informative prior distribution I assumed that the prior follow a similar distribtuion as the given data so I set the mean of the prior beta distribution to p_hat and solved for beta. I used this information to construct a df with possible alpha and beta combinations. I then used the standard deviation from the data to find the alpha and beta that best fit the data.
For the second informative prior distribution I used the information given from the sports announcer. I solved for alpha and beta using the target mean. To find the combination of alpha and beta that best fits the sports announcer’s guess I solved for the alpha and beta that have as close as possible to 5% chance of the proportion of serves being less than 70%. I chose 5% because of the announcer’s wording of being “almost sure”. I believe any number between 2% and 15% would be a reasonable guess. This is a weakness of bayesian models, the priors can be subjective and different priors can lead to very different results.

Priors Plot

ggplot(data = prior_plot_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")






Posteriors Plot
To obtain my posteriors I used the fact we saw in class that if you have a beta prior and binomial data, the posterior distribution is Beta(alpha_post = alpha_prior + yobs, beta_post = n - yobs + beta_prior)
From the data I see that yobs = 56 and that n = 84. I then apply this equation to all three of my priors to obtain the three posteriors.

ggplot(data = posterior_plot_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")




I used the alpha and beta for each posterior to calculate the posterior mean in the following way: alpha / alpha + beta
Posterior means:
Non-informative posterior mean: 0.6627907 Informative posterior mean 1: 0.6801075 Informative Posterior mean 2: 0.7265388
I used the qbeta function to obtain the 90% credible intervals which can be found in the code above.
Non-informative 90% credible interval for p: (0.5772453, 0.7440061) Informative 1 90% credible interval for p: (0.6160421, 0.7414111) Informative 2 90% credible interval for p: (0.6832283, 0.7681138)
There is a 90% probability that Nadal wins between 57.7 and 74.4% of the points when he’s serving on clay if we use the non_informative prior. The interval is 61.6% to 74.1% if we use data from the past match against Djokovic to construct our prior and 68.3% to 76.8% if we use the sports announcer’s estimate and a 5% “small number” to construct our prior.
The posteriors are different from each other because they have different prior distributions that are assuming different things about Nadal’s ability to win points on his serve. I would probably choose the second posterior because I think that it makes the most sense to base thge prior on actual data. However, I would prefer to have more than one data point to base my prior on. The data used might not be representative of Nadal’s ability to hold his serve against other players than Djokovic or even agisnt other matches against Djokovic. Even with these caveats I believe it’s the best prior because it contains more information than the non_informative prior. The second informative prior could be a good choice but I don’t like the subjectivity of choosing a “almost sure” number and how big the difference is in alphas and betas based of different “small numbers”.
I think the second informative posterior has a lower variance than the other two because we kind of artificially create this low variance by restricting the prior model to have a low probability, in my case 5% that the proportion of points won on serve is less than 70%. This will give the prior a low variance which we can also see in the posterior.
In this project, I found three different bayesian models that try to predict what proportion of points Nadal will win on his serve when playing on clay. By trying three different prior distributions, I can compre my assumptions and the resulting posteriors and choose the model I deem best. We see that the models predict that Nadal will win between 66.3 and 72.6% of the points on his serve.
